description: BINARY STARS brings together two students from METU Northern Cyprus Campus and Bursa Technical University. We aim to create an interactive lunar mission trainer that helps young learners explore decisions about power, food, life support and radiation protection. Our focus is accessible design, scientific accuracy and learning through play.
summary: Binary Stars - Planet Ops is a Turkish/English resource-decision game designed for junior explorers. Players visit eight fictional orbital stations from Neptune to Mercury, alongside separate Moon, Mars and Mercury surface missions. Distinct tasks connect oxygen, power, timing, protection and food. Version 0.36 adds clearer three-milestone mission feedback, actual paid-job progress and explanations when work is waiting for a required condition. Its refreshed interface uses the team’s existing gold two-star orbital logo. Players compare work methods, inspect their actual result and revise the next plan. NASA planetary references and archived ISS plant-study metadata provide context; game times, costs and hazards remain authored abstractions. Playable browser and editable Godot versions are available. Educational effectiveness has not yet been measured with learners.
details:
Binary Stars - Planet Ops responds to the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by making connected resource decisions visible through play. It is designed for the challenge's intended ages 7-12, with Turkish and English interfaces.

The Solar Expedition follows eight fictional orbital work decks: Neptune, Uranus, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Earth, Venus and Mercury. Their missions cover cargo transport, relay alignment, drone escort, observation timing, a greenhouse chain, air-leak repair, a pressure probe and moving shade. Separate Moon, Mars and Mercury surface missions remain playable. The orbital stations do not imply walkable surfaces on gas or ice giants.

Before starting, players compare economical and fast jobs. Fast work saves work time at a higher upfront power cost. Travelling and waiting continue to consume oxygen. Optional exploration, repairs, stored oxygen and fictional suit support create additional choices. Help, planning and journals pause the simulation. Solid obstacles require movement and jumping; local action guidance distinguishes the next goal from the action currently available nearby.

Solar Mars processes ice and water, powers crop lighting, harvests and packs food. In the separate surface Mars mission, produced water is allocated between food production and a base reserve. These modes have different recipes and timers. A mission result records the actual attempt; Change Plan prepares a new briefing. Journals encourage prediction and reflection without grading learners or claiming that better game statistics prove learning. In v0.36, the Solar Expedition shows three actual objective milestones and highlights the next required step. Uranus explicitly follows relay order 2 → 1 → 3. Paid jobs display completed work, remaining required work time and the power already paid. If a required mission condition blocks work, progress stops and a waiting reason is shown; oxygen use and field hazards continue. These indicators follow the real job state through waiting, pause, cancellation and retry. The mission board uses the team’s existing gold two-star orbital logo and makes the next available mission prominent.

Godot 4/GDScript and Canvas2D/JavaScript use shared JSON mission content. The v0.36 release passed 749 browser checks and 3,444 native checks, including focused tests for the new job and milestone feedback. These are software checks, not evidence of learner outcomes. The linked 29-second demo and seven-slide PDF remain historical v0.33 materials and do not show the v0.36 interface. The video presents a genuine automated Neptune route at about 2.5x speed; that mission took 52.7 game seconds.

NASA resources provide context rather than a calibrated engineering model. Approximate Sun distances are not live positions, and growth, heat, risk, pressure and resource rates use authored game scales. Communication delay is not quantitatively simulated. Learner testing, accessibility evaluation and measured educational effectiveness remain future evaluation work.

AI ASSISTANCE AND DEVELOPMENT HISTORY

Yes. ChatGPT and Codex were used extensively to propose and refine features, generate and modify JavaScript/GDScript, debug failures, create tests, translate text, research and summarize public references, and draft project materials. AI also contributed solution refinements; we do not describe the project or its idea provenance as independently unaided human work. The team supplied iterative requirements, priorities and feedback. Individual coding contributions have not been assigned or independently verified.

The demo contains real production-game captures, with AI-generated title cards, captions and editing visibly marked in the picture. "Soft Orbit" is original AI-generated instrumental music created through an explicit note recipe and PCM synthesis for this video. Music generation is acknowledged in the viewing-page description, video credits and MP4 metadata. Kenney CC0 effects are separate credited samples. No generated replacement gameplay, personal voice or identifiable person is used.

Code/data provenance, source mappings, asset licences and model limits accompany the source package. NASA logos, flags or mission branding were not added to the generated demo artwork.

Available development history includes work on 13 November 2026, before the published 14 November event opening. That history is disclosed, not re-dated. The organisers must determine how the pre-event work and AI contributions affect this entry's eligibility. No organiser eligibility ruling is claimed.

NASA DATA AND EDUCATIONAL USE

NASA Science planet pages and NASA fact sheets supply curated planet facts, outer-to-inner order and rounded average Sun distances. These are static educational references, not live telemetry or current orbital positions. The source package maps facts to their URLs.

We consulted NASA OSDR study OSD-267 / VEG-01A, "Microbiological and nutritional analysis of lettuce crops grown on the International Space Station-VEG01A", DOI 10.26030/0cpc-g985. Archived metadata were accessed on 14 November 2026. The protocol's harvest after 33 days and 16-hour light / 8-hour dark cycle provide a concrete comparison for the food-production lesson in the educational companion.

Those conditions describe that ISS experiment, not a universal crop constant or a Mars crop result. We did not analyze raw assay data, connect a live NASA API, or fit the game's crop timers, energy costs or hazards to the study. OSDR is used as a traceable educational resource, not as a claim of automatic award eligibility.

Additional context: NASA Veggie plant hardware and space-radiation explanations.

TOOLS, LICENCES AND OTHER REFERENCES

Original project code and code-drawn geometric artwork: MIT; see LICENSE in the source package.

Godot Engine 4: MIT.

Game fonts: DejaVu Sans / Bold / Mono with their distributed DejaVu/Bitstream notices.

Game effects: Kenney Sci-Fi Sounds, Interface Sounds and RPG Audio, CC0 1.0. Author/pack notices and a per-file processing/hash manifest are retained.

Demo music: "Soft Orbit", original AI-generated synthesized instrumental created for this project; no third-party music recording or voice was used. Video credits and machine-readable metadata accompany the demo.

Presentation design and space illustrations: the team's supplied Canva PDF template. Real gameplay/result images were captured from the current Godot production scene. The seven-slide PDF is an alternative demo included in this delivery; it is not an editable PowerPoint file. The replacement body text uses Poor Story (SIL Open Font License); its notice is included.

Development and media tools include ChatGPT/Codex, Python, Node.js, NumPy, Pillow, FFmpeg, ReportLab and PDF-processing tools. Their use is disclosed rather than represented as an independent authorship or endorsement claim. NASA materials are separately attributed in the NASA Data field; no additional space-agency dataset is claimed. Retain the asset-specific notices supplied with the project.

TEAM IDENTITY AND CURRENT SOURCE

The existing team-page PNG logo is reused unchanged. The compact orbital SVG emblem was adapted with Codex assistance. Logo source, checksum and asset-specific scope are recorded in docs/BRAND.txt in the source package; the team logo is separate from the original-code MIT licence. The current editable v0.36 Godot and browser source is available at https://binary-stars-lunar-ops.opalclay1.chatgpt.site/downloads/Binary-Stars-Godot-Prototype.zip
